note: Daily life on the Marunouchi-Ginza map (issue #357): the people to know, their hours, the jobs, the counters and the calendar. Built into web/data/tokyo/life.json by pipeline/life.py, which resolves every place. Facts in 'fact' are checked against published sources; each event names its own in 'source'.

fares.note: What a ride costs (web/game/fares.js). JR East's adult IC fare for 1 to 3 km after its revision of 14 March 2026 (155 yen by IC card, 160 by ticket; before it 146 and 150), from Traffic News and Impress Watch: JR East's own pages refused the request, so check it there when they answer. The water buses have no fare here: neither Tokyo Cruise nor the Tokyo Mizube Line sells a ticket between these piers today (Hamarikyu is a landing from Asakusa only, and the Mizube Line's reduced network of 17 October 2026 does not call at them).

card.name: Suica
card.text: Touch in at the gate and out at the other end. An IC card pays to the yen; a paper ticket is rounded up to ten.

bonds.title: The attendant at the gates

places.where: Yurakucho's gates, covering the lunch hour

bonds.busy: I'm on the gates for the evening rush now. Find me out here on the plaza in the morning or the daytime.

ranks.title: 335 metres of brick
ranks.invite: You looked up at the domes before you looked for your platform. Have you a little of the {slot}? Let me show you my building.
talk: Look left, then right. Three hundred and thirty-five metres of brick, end to end. Tatsuno Kingo drew it, and it opened in December 1914.
The fires of May 1945 took the domes and the third floor. For sixty years we made do with plain roofs. The domes you see came back in 2012.
ranks.fact: Tokyo Station's Marunouchi building, by Tatsuno Kingo, opened in 1914 and is about 335 m long; its domes and third floor, lost to bombing in May 1945, were restored in 2012.

ask.q: Which way would you say the station faces?

options.reply: Yes. Straight down the avenue to the Palace. The middle doors were made for the Emperor, and they are still kept for the Imperial family.
Ginza is behind us and to the south. It faces the Palace, straight down the avenue; the middle doors were made for the Emperor.

request.text: Walk the avenue from the station to the Palace plaza
request.ask: Have you walked the avenue yet? Straight out from the middle doors to the Palace plaza. Then look back at us.

ranks.title: A hundred shaku
talk: You looked back. Then you saw the ledge on the towers, about a third of the way up. Thirty-one metres: a hundred shaku, the old limit.
When the Maru Building was rebuilt in glass they kept that line, so the street still feels the height it was in my grandfather's day.
The drivers in the rotary hand me lost umbrellas all year. I've told them you're a friend of the station.
ranks.fact: The Marunouchi Building, rebuilt in 2002, keeps a podium at 31 m, the hundred-shaku height limit that shaped the district until the 1960s.

gives.name: A word at the taxi rank
gives.text: 30% off every taxi and ride in central Tokyo

request.text: Eat something from a counter: a station lunch box will do
request.ask: Have you eaten? There's an ekiben stand by the gates. A railway runs on its lunch boxes.

ranks.title: Up and down
talk: Good. Next time eat it on the train, before the first stop. That's the rule.
This is where the main lines begin: there are zero-kilometre posts on the platforms. About four thousand trains a day, more than any other station in Japan.
And every train coming toward Tokyo is an 'up' train, wherever it starts.
ranks.fact: Tokyo Station is the starting point of Japan's main lines, marked by zero-kilometre posts on its platforms, and handles about 4,000 trains a day.

ask.q: So a train from here to Aomori, far to the north: up or down?

options.reply: Down. Everything leaving Tokyo is a down train, north or south. Point at the board and say it aloud: you'll never board the wrong one.
North has nothing to do with it. Toward Tokyo is up, away is down, whichever way the compass points.

request.text: See the station's brick lit, after dark
request.ask: Come back to the plaza after dark, when the brick is lit. I see it on every night shift and I still stop.

ranks.title: Eight of the twelve
talk: You saw it lit. Now go in under the north dome one day and look up.
Eight eagles, and eight animals of the zodiac. Only eight: the rat, the rabbit, the horse and the rooster are missing.
They turned up in Kyushu, on a hot-spring gate by the same architect. Nobody knows whether he meant it as a joke.
ranks.fact: Each dome of Tokyo Station carries eight eagles and eight of the twelve zodiac animals; the missing four are carved on Tatsuno Kingo's gate at Takeo Onsen in Saga.

request.ask: Keep walking. When you can tell me which exit faces the Palace without looking at a sign, come back.

ranks.title: Pointing and calling
talk: Point at the signal. Say it aloud: 'Signal clear.' It feels foolish for a week, and then you can't cross a road without it.
I point at everything now. The kettle. The front door. My mother finds it very funny.
Do one thing properly and say so out loud. That's all I know, and it keeps a great many trains apart.
ranks.fact: Japanese railway staff point at signals and call their state aloud, shisa kanko; a 1994 railway study found the habit cut mistakes by about 85 per cent.

gives.name: The station's good name
gives.text: 15% more for every job in central Tokyo

bonds.title: The grill under the tracks
bonds.busy: The charcoal's cold till five. Come in the evening, when the trains bring the offices down.

ranks.title: Under the tracks
ranks.invite: いらっしゃい! You look like you've walked. Got the {slot}? Sit by the fire.
talk: Feel that? The Yamanote Line, right over the grill. These arches are red brick, built for the elevated railway that opened in 1910.
A German engineer laid out the viaduct, so they say it's Berlin under here. I say Berlin never smelled this good.
ranks.fact: The red-brick viaduct at Yurakucho carried Tokyo's first elevated railway from 1910, laid out with the German engineer Franz Baltzer on the model of Berlin's Stadtbahn.

ask.q: Why did the bars come to live under a railway, d'you think?

options.text: It was cheap, and nobody minds the smoke
options.reply: Exactly. No neighbours upstairs but trains, and trains don't complain.
Ha! The view is a brick wall. No: it was cheap, and the only neighbours upstairs are trains.

request.ask: You haven't eaten. I can tell by how you look at the grill. Order something, anywhere, then talk to me.

ranks.title: A box for Ginza
talk: You've eaten. Now you can work.
Yurakucho. They say it's named for Urakusai, a tea master, the warlord Nobunaga's brother, who had a house by the moat here. True or not, it's a good name for somewhere to drink.
A box of skewers for Yui's office in Ginza: she orders for the whole floor when they work late. Fast, and level.
ranks.fact: Yurakucho is traditionally said to take its name from Oda Urakusai, a tea master and younger brother of Oda Nobunaga, who is said to have had a mansion here.

gives.name: Ishikawa's runner
gives.text: A paid delivery from the grill, in your diary under Work

request.text: Run the skewers to Yui at Ginza 4-chome
request.ask: The box is tied and going cold. It's in your diary, under Work.

ranks.title: This was the sea
talk: Yui says they were hot. She said it with her mouth full.
You know this was the sea? Four hundred years ago Hibiya was an inlet of the bay. The first shogun had a hill cut down in Kanda and tipped it in.
The Palace plaza, Hibiya Park, my arches: all of it stands on that fill. Tokyo forgets. I don't.
ranks.fact: Hibiya was an inlet of Edo Bay until the early 1600s, when Tokugawa Ieyasu had it filled with earth cut from Kanda's hill; Hibiya Park and the Palace plaza stand on that fill.

ask.q: So where's the nearest salt water now?

options.reply: Good! A tidal pond: the bay comes in through a sluice. Sea fish in a garden, twenty minutes' walk from my grill.
Nearer than that. The pond at Hamarikyu is tidal: the bay comes in through a sluice, twenty minutes' walk from here.

request.text: Ride a water bus on the bay
request.ask: Have you been out on the water yet? The water bus leaves from Hamarikyu. Go on: I'll keep your seat.

ranks.title: The bridge that went
talk: You smell of the bay. Good.
Between here and Ginza there was a moat, and a bridge over it: Sukiyabashi. Lovers met on it in a radio serial the whole country stopped to hear.
In 1958 they filled the moat and built an expressway where the water was. The crossing kept the bridge's name. That's Tokyo: the name stays, the water goes.
ranks.fact: Sukiyabashi, the bridge between Yurakucho and Ginza, was removed in 1958 when the outer moat was filled for the Tokyo Expressway; the crossing keeps its name.

gives.name: The master's tongue
gives.text: Taste: you know a good counter when you smell one

ranks.title: A counter is a promise
talk: Since 1985, this grill. Same arch, same fire.
My father said a counter is a promise: whoever sits down, you feed. Minister or mop-man, same skewer, same price.
You've a place at mine. Come when it rains: the arch drips at the door and it's dry by the fire.
ranks.fact: Yurakucho Station opened on the elevated line in June 1910, four years before Tokyo Station, its neighbour to the north.

gives.name: A place at the counter
gives.text: 20% more for every job in central Tokyo

bonds.title: The water-bus captain
bonds.busy: I'm taking her out on the evening run. Find me on the landing in the morning or the daytime.

ranks.title: Where the river ends
ranks.invite: You're watching the tide, not the boats. Have you some of the {slot}? Come to the rail.
talk: That's the Sumida coming down on the left, and the bay opening on the right. When the shoguns kept this garden it sat right at the river's mouth.
The pond behind those pines is sea water. A sluice opens with the tide, and the pond rises and falls with the bay. It's the only one left in Tokyo.
ranks.fact: Hamarikyu's Shioiri-no-ike is the only tidal seawater pond left in Tokyo's Edo-period gardens: a sluice lets Tokyo Bay in and out with the tide.

ask.q: What lives in a garden pond like that, would you say?

options.reply: Right. Mullet, young sea bass, gobies, eels. And crabs on the stones at low water.
Not in salt water. Mullet, young sea bass, gobies and eels, and crabs on the stones at low water.

request.text: Ride a water bus from one pier to another
request.ask: You can't know a harbour from the shore. Ride one of the boats to another pier, then come and tell me what you saw.

ranks.title: The shogun's ducks
talk: You've been out. You stand differently.
There are two duck grounds in this garden, from 1778 and 1791. Narrow ditches off a pond, a decoy duck, a man behind a bank with a net.
The ducks still winter here. Nobody has netted one in a long while.
ranks.fact: Hamarikyu keeps two Edo-period duck-hunting grounds, Koshindo of 1778 and Shinsenza of 1791, where wild ducks were lured up narrow ditches by decoys.

gives.name: A captain's routes
gives.text: Lines: you read a timetable like a tide table

request.ask: Ride some more. Boats, cabs, whatever moves. Come back when you know which pier is which.

ranks.title: The pine
talk: By the main gate there's a black pine the sixth shogun, Ienobu, had planted in 1709, when he remade the garden. Three hundred years old, and wider than my boat is long.
They prop its branches on posts now. A garden is a slow boat: somebody has to keep it trim for a captain he'll never meet.
ranks.fact: The 300-year pine by Hamarikyu's main gate was planted in 1709, when the sixth shogun, Tokugawa Ienobu, remodelled the garden.

gives.name: The river's weather
gives.text: The diary shows the next day hour by hour, and Captain Aoki writes when rain is coming
gives.tip: The water-buses run in the rain. The windows are big.

request.text: Take one photograph at golden or blue hour (photo mode, O)
request.ask: The bay's at its best when the sun is low. Take one picture in that light, anywhere, and show me.

ranks.title: The bridge that opened
talk: Good light. And you held it level: most people tilt the bay.
Upstream from here is Kachidoki Bridge, 1940. The middle used to lift for ships, both leaves, five times a day.
It last opened in 1970. The machinery is still in the piers. Every captain on this water would give a month's pay to see it go up once.
ranks.fact: Kachidoki Bridge, the bascule bridge near the mouth of the Sumida, opened in 1940 and last raised its two leaves for shipping in November 1970.

gives.name: The captain's good word
gives.text: 15% more for every job in central Tokyo

ranks.title: Follow the water
talk: Thirty years on this run. People think it's the same trip every day.
It never is. The tide, the wind off the bay, a tower where there was a crane. I watched the whole of Shiodome go up from this wheel.
When you're lost in this city, find the water and follow it. It all comes down here in the end.
ranks.fact: Shiodome, behind Hamarikyu, was the site of Shimbashi Station, the terminus of Japan's first railway in 1872; its goods yard closed in 1986 and the towers followed in the early 2000s.

gives.name: Follow the water
gives.text: Bearings, from someone who steers by them

bonds.title: The guide at the tower
bonds.busy: I've a group going up the stairs. I'm free in the evening and at night, when the tower's lit.

ranks.title: Thirteen metres
ranks.invite: Everyone cranes their neck. You're counting the cross-braces. Got the {slot}?
talk: 333 metres, finished in December 1958. Thirteen more than the Eiffel Tower, on little more than half the metal: about four thousand tonnes of steel.
Naito Tachu designed it. They called him Doctor Tower: Nagoya's, Osaka's Tsutenkaku, then this.
ranks.fact: Tokyo Tower, designed by Naito Tachu and finished in December 1958, stands 333 m tall on about 4,000 tonnes of steel, little more than half the weight of the Eiffel Tower's ironwork.

ask.q: Why orange and white, do you think?

options.text: So that aircraft can see it
options.reply: Right: aviation rules. International orange and white, in bands. It's repainted by hand about every five years, and it takes a year.

options.text: To look like a shrine gate
options.reply: Nice idea, but it's aviation rules: international orange and white, so pilots see it. Repainted by hand about every five years.

request.text: Photograph the tower from close by (photo mode, O)
request.ask: Take me a picture of it from down here. Photo mode. Closer than you think is right.

ranks.title: Winter orange
talk: Good. Everyone else shoots it from too far away.
It has been lit this way since 1989, by a lighting designer called Ishii Motoko: warm orange through the cold months, a cooler white in summer.
I photograph it most nights for the tower's noticeboard. Here: I've set your camera the way I set mine.
ranks.fact: Tokyo Tower's Landmark Light, by the lighting designer Ishii Motoko, dates from 1989: a warm orange in the colder months and a cooler white in summer.

gives.name: Night film
gives.text: Photographs after sunset come out on Ren's night stock

request.text: Walk down to Zojoji, the temple below the tower
request.ask: Have you been down to Zojoji? Five minutes downhill. Stand in front of the hall and turn round.

ranks.title: The shoguns' temple
talk: So you saw the picture everyone wants: the old hall with the tower behind it.
Six of the fifteen Tokugawa shoguns are buried there. And the great red gate on the street is from 1622. It came through the earthquake and the air raids.
ranks.fact: Zojoji, below Tokyo Tower, holds the graves of six Tokugawa shoguns; its gate, the Sangedatsumon of 1622, is one of the oldest wooden buildings in Tokyo.

ask.q: How many times do they ring its bell at New Year?

options.reply: A hundred and eight: one for each worldly desire. The bell is from 1673 and weighs fifteen tonnes. You feel it in your teeth.
A hundred and eight, one for each worldly desire. The bell is from 1673, fifteen tonnes: you feel it in your teeth.

request.text: Guess a building's height to within a quarter (G)
request.ask: Try your eye on something first: pick a building, press G, and tell me how close you were.

ranks.title: Six hundred steps
talk: Near enough. Now your legs: about six hundred steps to the main deck, 150 metres up, in the open air with orange steel all round you.
Children do it in fifteen minutes. Office workers take twenty and blame their shoes.
From the top deck, at 250 metres, on a clear winter morning: Fuji, the bay, and the whole plain.
ranks.fact: An open-air stair of about 600 steps climbs from the roof of Tokyo Tower's Foot Town to the main deck, 150 m up; the top deck is at 250 m.

gives.name: A guide's eye
gives.text: Eye: you size a tower up from its foot

ranks.title: The second tower
talk: In 2012 a taller tower opened across the river, 634 metres, and took over the television. People asked me whether we'd close.
We didn't. Nobody proposes under the other one.
A city keeps what it loves, not what's tallest. Tell that to the next person who asks you the way to the new tower. Then send them here.
ranks.fact: Tokyo Skytree, 634 m tall, opened in 2012 and took over most television broadcasting from Tokyo Tower the following year.

gives.name: A guide's introduction
gives.text: 25% more for every job in central Tokyo

jobs.title: A pot of tare to Shimbashi
jobs.blurb: Ishikawa's sauce pot, lent to a friend's stall under the arches at Shimbashi. One stop south on the Yamanote line.
jobs.text: A lidded clay pot, heavy, wrapped in a furoshiki. "Southbound, towards Shinagawa. Don't tip it."
jobs.done: Under the Shimbashi arches a man in a headband lifts the lid and breathes in. "Thirty years of it. Tell him thanks."

jobs.title: Which way from the Palace plaza?
jobs.blurb: Visitors on the gravel ask the way. Face each place's true bearing; the nearer, the better the pay.
jobs.who: A visitor with a folded map
jobs.done: They bow, and set off the right way.

jobs.title: Brick and glass
jobs.blurb: A railway magazine wants the station and the three towers that bought the air above it. Photo mode (O); golden or blue hour pays a quarter more.
jobs.done: The picture editor writes back: 'The brick one for the cover.'

jobs.title: Skewers for Ginza
jobs.blurb: A box from Ishikawa-san's grill under the Yurakucho tracks to Yui's office at Ginza 4-chome, while they are hot.
jobs.text: Thirty skewers for the fourth floor. Keep the box level.
jobs.done: Yui signs for the whole floor.

jobs.title: Programmes for the Kabuki-za
jobs.blurb: A bundle of printed programmes from Ginza 4-chome down Harumi-dori to the theatre, before the afternoon house goes in.
jobs.text: Two hundred programmes, still smelling of ink. The doors open at half past.

jobs.title: A fare to Tokyo Tower
jobs.blurb: Drive your own car as a cab: pick up at the kerb by the station plaza and take your passenger past the Palace and Hibiya to the foot of the tower.
jobs.at_name: the kerb by the station plaza
jobs.who: A grandmother up from Sendai, with her grandson
jobs.text: "The tower, please. He has never seen it lit."

shops.name: Yakitori under the tracks ガード下
shops.hello: いらっしゃい! Sit anywhere. Beer crates are chairs.

menu.name: Negima, two skewers
menu.text: Chicken thigh and leek, turn about, over charcoal, while a train goes over the arch. The leek is there to cut the fat.

menu.name: Tsukune
menu.text: A minced chicken skewer, glazed with the sweet soy sauce the pot has held for years, with a raw yolk to dip it in.

menu.name: Motsu nikomi
menu.text: Offal stewed in miso with daikon and konnyaku: the dish the stalls under these arches fed the office crowd on after the war.

shops.name: Ekiben stand 駅弁
shops.where: Tokyo Station, by the Marunouchi gates
shops.hello: Good day. Which train are you taking?

menu.name: Makunouchi ekiben
menu.text: Rice in neat barrels, grilled salmon, a rolled omelette, fish cake, simmered vegetables. The station lunch box is as old as the long-distance train: the first are said to have been sold at Utsunomiya in 1885.

menu.name: A station stamp book
menu.text: A pocket notebook for the ink stamps stations keep by their gates. The custom began at Fukui Station in 1931, and collectors still queue for a clean impression.

shops.name: Kissaten 喫茶店
shops.hello: Good morning. The set, or just coffee?

menu.name: Morning set
menu.text: Thick toast, a boiled egg and coffee dripped through flannel, served until eleven. The morning set is the old coffee shops' bargain: the food comes for the price of the coffee, or little more.

menu.name: Cream soda
menu.text: Bright green melon soda with a ball of vanilla ice cream and one red cherry. The coffee shops have served it this way for the best part of a century.

shops.name: The bakery at 4-chome パン屋
shops.hello: Irasshaimase. The cherry ones are just out.

menu.name: Sakura anpan
menu.text: A soft bun raised with sake yeast, filled with sweet bean paste, a salted cherry blossom pressed into the top. Anpan was first baked in Ginza in 1874, and this one was made for the Emperor Meiji the spring after.

menu.name: Fruit sandwich
menu.text: Strawberries and whipped cream in soft white bread with the crusts cut off: the fruit parlours of Ginza made a neat lunch of dessert.

events.title: New Year greeting at the Palace
events.verb: Join the queue for the main gate
events.text: On 2 January the Palace's inner grounds open, and the Emperor and the Imperial family greet the crowd from a balcony, five times in most years.
lines: The gravel plaza is roped into lanes. Bags are checked, paper flags are handed out, and the queue moves toward the main gate and over the stone bridge.
Inside, the Emperor and the family come out on the glazed balcony of the Chowaden hall: five times in most years, from about ten past ten until twenty past two.
It is one of two days in the year when anyone may walk in through the main gate. The other is the Emperor's birthday, 23 February.

events.title: Night cherries at Chidorigafuchi
events.text: About 260 cherry trees along 700 metres of the moat, lit from sunset while they flower: late March to early April in most years.
lines: The path along the moat is one-way tonight, and nobody minds. The branches reach down over the water and the lamps make them white against the dark.
About 260 trees along 700 metres. Below, rowing boats drift under the branches; the queue for one is longer than the path.
The lights come on at sunset for as long as the flowers last: the end of March and the first days of April, in most years.

events.title: Sanno Matsuri: the procession in Ginza
events.text: Hie Shrine's great festival, held in full in even-numbered years: some five hundred people in court dress walk the city centre for a day. In 2026 the procession was on 12 June.
lines: Traffic stops, and Ginza hears wooden clogs. Two phoenix palanquins, a portable shrine, floats, men on horseback: three hundred metres of the Heian court, passing the department stores.
It left Hie Shrine this morning and has been to the Palace gate, where the priests go in to pray, and round by Tokyo Station and Nihonbashi. About five hundred people walk all day.
The full festival comes every other year, in even years, turn about with Kanda's. In 2026 the procession fell on 12 June.

events.title: Marunouchi Illumination
events.native: 丸の内イルミネーション
events.text: The street trees of Naka-dori, 1.2 kilometres of them, strung with champagne-gold lights from 16:00, from mid November to mid February.
lines: Every tree on the street is wound to its twigs in one colour: a pale gold the organisers call champagne. Office workers slow down, which they never do.
About 250 trees along 1.2 kilometres of Naka-dori, lit from four in the afternoon. It runs from mid November to mid February: in 2026, from 12 November.

events.title: The New Year's bell at Zojoji
events.text: At midnight Zojoji's great bell of 1673 is struck 108 times, with Tokyo Tower lit behind the hall.
lines: From eleven a fire burns in the yard for last year's charms. The crowd fills the steps of the hall, and the tower stands orange behind the roof.
At midnight the first stroke. The bell was cast in 1673 and weighs fifteen tonnes; it is rung a hundred and eight times, once for each worldly desire.
People with tickets take the rope in turns. Everyone else counts, loses count, and starts the year anyway.
